# Standards catalog

<!-- Generated by `npm run docs` from packages/core/src/controls. Do not edit by hand. -->

20 deterministic controls. Each one is a pure function of the repository contents: no network calls, no model output.
A control returns **pass**, **fail**, **n/a** (does not apply to this repo) or **unknown** (could not be decided; never counted as a failure).

Default mode is where a control starts in the audit → warn → enforce rollout; a repo can override it per control in `.codex-loop.yml`.

| ID | Control | Category | Severity | Default mode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CDX-001 | README exists and explains the project | hygiene | low | warn |
| CDX-002 | CODEOWNERS defines who reviews changes | hygiene | medium | warn |
| CDX-003 | Security policy tells people how to report vulnerabilities | hygiene | low | audit |
| CDX-004 | License is declared | hygiene | low | audit |

| CDX-012 | GitHub workflows declare least-privilege permissions | ci | medium | warn |
| CDX-020 | Dependency lockfiles are committed | supply-chain | medium | warn |
| CDX-021 | Automated dependency updates are configured | supply-chain | low | audit |
| CDX-040 | Docker base images are tagged or pinned | containers | medium | warn |

## CDX-001: README exists and explains the project

**Why.** A README is the first thing humans and coding agents read. Without it, every newcomer (and every agent session) has to rediscover what the project is and how to run it.

**Fix.** Add a README.md at the repository root covering what the project does, how to run it, and how to test it.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Keep README.md accurate: update it in the same change when setup steps, commands or behavior change.

## CDX-002: CODEOWNERS defines who reviews changes

**Why.** Code review only works when the right people are asked. CODEOWNERS routes reviews automatically and makes ownership explicit, which matters more as agents raise the volume of changes.

**Fix.** Add .github/CODEOWNERS mapping paths to the teams or people who own them.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Respect CODEOWNERS: keep changes scoped to one area where possible so the right owners can review them.

## CDX-003: Security policy tells people how to report vulnerabilities

**Why.** Without a documented reporting path, vulnerabilities get reported publicly or not at all. (An organization-level .github repository can supply this; if so, record an exception.)

**Fix.** Add SECURITY.md describing supported versions and how to report a vulnerability privately.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Never put secrets, tokens or exploit details in code, commits, issues or logs; follow SECURITY.md for reporting.

## CDX-004: License is declared

**Why.** A missing license leaves reuse rights undefined, which blocks adoption and complicates compliance reviews.

**Fix.** Add a LICENSE file, or record an exception for private repositories where it is intentionally absent.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Do not copy code from sources whose license is unknown or incompatible with this repository's license.

## CDX-010: Continuous integration is configured

**Why.** Changes that are not built and tested automatically reach main on trust alone; the cost of each regression lands on whoever finds it.

**Fix.** Add a CI workflow (for example .github/workflows/ci.yml) that installs, builds and tests on every pull request.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Make sure CI passes before proposing a change; never disable or skip CI checks to make a change pass.

## CDX-011: GitHub Actions are pinned to full commit SHAs

**Why.** A tag like @v4 can be moved by whoever controls the action's repository. Pinning to a full commit SHA means a compromised upstream cannot silently change what runs in your pipeline with your secrets.

**Fix.** Replace `uses: owner/action@v4` with `uses: owner/action@<40-char-sha> # v4`. Dependabot and Renovate can keep the SHAs current.

**Rule given to coding agents.** When adding or editing GitHub Actions, pin every `uses:` to a full 40-character commit SHA with a version comment.

## CDX-012: GitHub workflows declare least-privilege permissions

**Why.** Without an explicit `permissions:` block, the workflow token may get broad default write access. A compromised step or dependency can then push code or tamper with releases.

**Fix.** Add top-level `permissions: contents: read` to each workflow and grant more only to the jobs that need it.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Every workflow you write declares `permissions:` explicitly, read-only by default; grant write access per job only when required.

## CDX-020: Dependency lockfiles are committed

**Why.** Without a lockfile every install can resolve different versions. Builds stop being reproducible and a malicious or broken release of any transitive dependency flows straight into your artifact.

**Fix.** Commit the lockfile for your package manager (package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, yarn.lock, go.sum, poetry.lock, uv.lock, Cargo.lock, ...).

**Rule given to coding agents.** Commit lockfile changes together with any dependency change, and never delete a lockfile to work around an install error.

## CDX-021: Automated dependency updates are configured

**Why.** Dependencies that only change when someone remembers accumulate known vulnerabilities. Automated update PRs keep the gap small and each change reviewable.

**Fix.** Add .github/dependabot.yml (or a Renovate config) covering your package ecosystems and GitHub Actions. If updates are configured at the organization level, record an exception.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Prefer the repository's existing dependency versions; when you must add a dependency, choose a maintained one and pin it through the lockfile.

## CDX-040: Docker base images are tagged or pinned

**Why.** `FROM node` or `FROM node:latest` builds a different image tomorrow than today. A specific tag (better: a digest) makes builds reproducible and lets scanners reason about what shipped.

**Fix.** Use a specific version tag such as `node:22-alpine`, or pin a digest with `@sha256:...`.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Never use `latest` or untagged Docker base images; pin a specific version tag or digest.

## CDX-041: Containers run as a non-root user

**Why.** A container that runs as root turns any application-level compromise into root inside the container, which makes escapes and lateral movement far easier.

**Fix.** Create an unprivileged user and switch to it in the final stage with `USER appuser`.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Final Docker stages must switch to a non-root `USER`; do not run application processes as root.

## CDX-050: Worker compatibility_date is current

**Why.** compatibility_date pins the Workers runtime behavior your code sees. A stale date means missing fixes and features, and a jump later is a larger, riskier change.

**Fix.** Set compatibility_date to a recent date (within 365 days) and test; update it as part of regular dependency upgrades.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Keep wrangler `compatibility_date` recent; do not lower it or remove compatibility flags without a reason recorded in the change.

## CDX-051: Worker observability is enabled

**Why.** A Worker without observability enabled is a black box in production: when it misbehaves there are no logs or traces to debug from.

**Fix.** Add `"observability": { "enabled": true }` to the Wrangler configuration.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Keep `observability.enabled` on in wrangler config, and log structured, secret-free events for errors.

## CDX-052: Wrangler [vars] contain no literal secrets

**Why.** `vars` in wrangler config are plain text and are committed with the repo. Secrets belong in `wrangler secret put` or Secrets Store, never in config.

**Fix.** Remove the value, rotate it, and set it with `wrangler secret put NAME` (or bind a Secrets Store secret). Keep only non-sensitive settings in `vars`.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Never put tokens, keys or passwords in wrangler `vars`; use `wrangler secret put` and reference the binding by name.

## CDX-060: TypeScript strict mode is enabled

**Why.** Strict mode turns a large class of runtime errors (null access, implicit any, unsound function types) into compile errors. It is far cheaper to adopt at the start than to retrofit.

**Fix.** Set `"strict": true` in tsconfig.json compilerOptions (explicitly, so behavior does not depend on the TypeScript version).

**Rule given to coding agents.** Write code that compiles under TypeScript `strict`; do not use `any` or `// @ts-ignore` to silence errors, fix the types.

## CDX-061: The project has automated tests

**Why.** Tests are the feedback loop that lets humans and coding agents change code with confidence. Without them every change is a guess, and agent-written changes most of all.

**Fix.** Add tests for the core behavior and a `test` script (or the language's standard runner) so CI and agents can run them with one command.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Add or update tests for every behavior change, run the project's test command before finishing, and never delete or skip tests to make a change pass.

## CDX-070: Coding agents have repository context

**Why.** Agents that start every session cold re-learn commands and conventions, and tend to invent them. A short AGENTS.md with build/test commands and the rules that matter removes most of that guessing.

**Fix.** Generate one with `codex-loop context --write`, then edit it. Keep it short and specific to this repo.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Read AGENTS.md first and keep it current when commands or conventions change.

## CDX-030: .gitignore keeps local environment files out of git

**Why.** Local .env files routinely hold real credentials. One `git add .` without an ignore rule is how most committed secrets happen.

**Fix.** Add `.env`, `.env.*` (with `!.env.example`) and, for Cloudflare Workers projects, `.dev.vars` to .gitignore.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Never commit .env or .dev.vars files; put real values in untracked local files and document variable names in .env.example.

## CDX-031: No credential files are committed

**Why.** Committed .env files, private keys and keystores live forever in git history and in every clone and fork.

**Fix.** Remove the file from the repository, rotate anything it contained, and add it to .gitignore. Rewriting history alone does not un-leak a secret.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Do not create or commit .env, .dev.vars, private keys, keystores or credential files; use .env.example with placeholder values.

## CDX-032: No high-confidence secrets in tracked files

**Why.** API keys and private keys in source are harvested by bots within minutes of being pushed to a public repository, and are reused by anyone with clone access to a private one.

**Fix.** Revoke and rotate the credential first, then remove it from the code and load it from the environment or a secrets manager.

**Rule given to coding agents.** Never write API keys, tokens or private keys into code, tests, docs, comments or examples; read them from environment variables.
